title: Two Sum in a Sorted Array
statement:
Given an array of integers `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order and an integer `target`, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to `target`.

Return them as a list `[i, j]` with `i < j`, using 0-based indices. You may assume exactly one solution exists, and you may not use the same element twice.
ambiguities: Are the indices 0-based or 1-based? (The statement says 0-based, but a candidate who checks is rewarded.)
Can the array contain duplicates or negative numbers?
Is the 'exactly one solution' guarantee something we should still defend against?
What is the size of the input — does an O(n log n) solution suffice, or is O(n) required?
followUps: The array is no longer sorted. What changes?
Find all unique pairs summing to target, not just one.
The array does not fit in memory. How would you approach it?
Extend to three numbers summing to target.

optimal.approach: Two pointers from both ends, moving the left pointer inward when the sum is too small and the right pointer inward when it is too large.

pitfalls: Reaching for a hash map out of habit — that is O(n) space when the sortedness gives you O(1).
Off-by-one when the two pointers meet.
Not stating that sortedness is the property being exploited.

tests.note: duplicate values adjacent to the answer

title: Valid Parentheses
statement:
Given a string `s` containing only the characters `(`, `)`, `{`, `}`, `[` and `]`, decide whether every bracket is closed by one of the same type, in the right order.

Return `True` if the string is valid, `False` otherwise.
ambiguities: Is the empty string valid? (It is here, but asking is the point.)
Can the string contain characters other than brackets?
How long can the input be — does that rule out recursion?
Should we report where the mismatch is, or only whether one exists?
followUps: Return the index of the first character that breaks the string.
The bracket pairs are supplied at runtime instead of being fixed. What changes?
Return the length of the longest valid bracket substring.

optimal.approach: Push every opening bracket onto a stack; on a closing bracket, pop and check the pair matches. Valid exactly when nothing mismatches and the stack ends empty.

pitfalls: Counting brackets instead of stacking them — that accepts "([)]", which is invalid.
Forgetting the leftover opening brackets at the end, so "(" reads as valid.
Popping an empty stack when a closing bracket arrives first.

tests.note: counting brackets instead of stacking accepts this

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement:
`prices[i]` is the price of a stock on day `i`. Choose one day to buy and a later day to sell.

Return the maximum profit you can make. If no profitable trade exists, return `0`.
ambiguities: Must we trade at all, or is doing nothing allowed? (It is — that is what the 0 means.)
Can we buy and sell on the same day?
Can prices be zero or negative?
What should an empty or single-day array return?
followUps: Unlimited transactions, one at a time. What changes?
Return the two days, not just the profit.

optimal.approach: One pass keeping the lowest price seen so far and the best profit achievable by selling today.

pitfalls: The nested double loop — correct, but O(n^2), and the whole point is the single pass.
Returning a negative number on a falling market instead of 0.
Selling before buying by tracking the global minimum and maximum independently.

tests.note: a falling market earns nothing, not a loss
one day: you cannot sell later
the global minimum comes after the best sell day

title: Number of Islands
statement:
Given a 2D grid of `1`s (land) and `0`s (water), return the number of islands.

An island is a group of `1`s connected horizontally or vertically. Assume the grid is surrounded by water on all sides.
ambiguities: Is diagonal adjacency considered connected?
May we mutate the input grid to mark visited cells, or must it be preserved?
Can the grid be empty or ragged?
How large can the grid get — does recursion risk a stack overflow?
followUps: Return the size of the largest island.
The grid does not fit in memory — how would you process it in chunks?
Cells are added one at a time; maintain the island count online (union-find).

optimal.space: O(rows * cols) worst case for the traversal frontier
optimal.approach: Scan every cell; on each unvisited land cell run a flood fill and increment the counter.

pitfalls: Not marking cells visited at enqueue time, so the same cell is queued repeatedly.
Index out of bounds on the grid edges.
Deep recursion on a large all-land grid blowing the stack.

title: Word Break
statement:
Given a string `s` and a list of words `word_dict`, return `True` if `s` can be segmented into a space-separated sequence of one or more dictionary words.

Words from the dictionary may be reused any number of times.
ambiguities: May a dictionary word be used more than once? (Yes here — worth confirming.)
Can the dictionary or the string be empty?
Are we case sensitive?
Do we need one valid segmentation, or just whether one exists?
followUps: Return every possible segmentation — what does that do to the complexity?
The dictionary has millions of words. What data structure now?

optimal.time: O(n^2 * m) where m is the max word length
optimal.approach: DP over prefixes: dp[i] is true when some j < i has dp[j] true and s[j:i] is in the dictionary.

pitfalls: Plain recursion without memoisation, which is exponential on inputs like 'aaaa...ab'.
Greedily taking the longest matching word, which is simply wrong.
Scanning the dictionary as a list instead of a set, adding a hidden linear factor.

title: Minimum Window Substring
statement:
Given strings `s` and `t`, return the shortest substring of `s` that contains every character of `t`, including duplicates.

If no such window exists, return the empty string `""`. Assume the answer is unique when one exists.
ambiguities: Does the window need the characters in order? (No — worth confirming out loud.)
How are duplicate characters in `t` counted?
What is the character set?
What should be returned when `t` is longer than `s`?
followUps: Return the start index instead of the substring.
What if `t` can contain characters absent from `s` entirely?
Find the longest window containing at most K distinct characters.

optimal.approach: Expand the right edge until the window is valid, then contract the left edge while it stays valid, tracking the best window. A `have`/`need` counter avoids rescanning the map.

pitfalls: Comparing the whole frequency map on every step, which makes it O(n * alphabet).
Mishandling duplicates in `t` — the window needs two 'a's, not one.
Forgetting to record the best window before contracting past it.

tests.note: t needs two 'a's, s has one
duplicates in t must all be covered
